newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lion seen driven by comparative valuation.
newsitem.headline: Lion seen driven by comparative valuation.

text.p: Lion Nathan Ltd's heady rally has been driven by a view that the brewer is cheap relative to its international peers, brokers and anlysts said on Wednesday.
While talk persists of a possible takeover, analysts viewed this as unlikely, given principal Douglas Myers' 16 percent stake and his often repeated statements that he is not a seller.
Another rumour dogging the firm is that it is about to start brewing Stella Artois under licence, but Lion spokesman Graham Seatter told Reuters last week the talk was ill-founded.
However, Seatter said Stella is a brand sold through its 50 percent-owned liquor chain, New Zealand Wines and Spirits, and sales of the Belgian brew had increased.
Analysts said it was more likely that NZ Wines and Spirits would re-position Stella's pricing to make it more attractive relative to the other top line lagers.
A news conference, scheduled for Thursday, is likely to announce such a move.
Lion is no stranger to takeover talk, which First NZ Capital broker Scott St John said was due to the company being a "conspicuous asset" with a relatively open share registry.
Lion traded today at NZ$4.05, just off last Friday's closing level of NZ$4.12 -- its highest point since February 1994.
"What the recent rally has done is essentially arbitrage the relative value gap between Lion and some of its offshore peers," St John said.

"If you looked at Lion Nathan when it was trading around the NZ$3.80 level the stock looked rather attractive on a comparative company basis," St John said. "On the back of that, there was a reasonable degree of buying generated," he said.
Lion would always attract takeover talk, but anyone wishing to buy the company would have to deal with Myers. The chances of Myers selling are rated by analysts as next to zero.
"He's said publicly that he's not a seller of his stock, but that would not necessarily preclude someone from being acquisitive," St John said.
"But the fact of the matter is that the recent rally has been valuation-driven. However, there has been an overlay of rumour and innuendo associated with potential takeover activity.
"It's a conspicuous asset in this part of the world with some very attractive positions and that will always drag some attention towards it," he said.
Lion had drawn broad-based offshore institutional buying interest from investors with a global perspective.
The most likely comparative model was Foster's Brewing Group Ltd, which competes with Lion in Australia, but others further afield were likely to have included in the mix.

"If you apply the average EBIT multiple for international brewers, one might come up with valuations of up to NZ$4.40 for Lion Nathan," St John said. "Overlaying that, you've had a relatively robust Australian share market which has seen their average market multiples climb steadily this year, which has also made brewing stocks look relatively attractive," he said.
Weakness in the New Zealand-Australian dollar had also driven valuations higher. One Sydney-based analyst agreed the comparative valuation scenario appeared the most likely driver.
Certainly, he said, the rally did not appear to be earnings driven, given the company's problems with its Pepsi franchise, which has struggled to break even on both sides of the Tasman.
Likewise, it would be some years yet before Lion's major China beer brewing initiative is proven successful, he said.
